E. 30 feet square, five years old

Total medical risk from a pond is total adult emergence per pond, not per unit area. That is area × realized per-area productivity. At constant 2 ft depth both water volume and wetted cement area scale with planform.

30 ft × 30 ft = 900 ft² surface vs 10 ft × 10 ft = 100 ft², ~9× surface and ~9× volume. Even at identical per-area performance the 30 ft basin will produce an order of magnitude more adults.

Age acts in the same direction for these artificial cement basins. Fresh concrete leaches Ca(OH)₂ and the water is strongly alkaline and biologically sterile for months. The first year is a chemical recovery phase as pH falls toward neutral and a periphyton/biofilm begins to establish on the vertical walls and bottom. By five years the surface is weathered, pH is stabilized, and there is a measurable accumulation of biofilm, fine detritus and algal accrual that provides larval food. That is exactly what is being reported in the field: older ponds have more established insect communities.

In a permanent cement basin with vertical sides and no macrophyte refuge, the limiting factor for a colonizing disease vector is not predator release, it is suitable chemistry and a persistent food base. Predator/competitor build-up such as odonate nymphs and dytiscids is constrained in a featureless concrete box and is far slower than the accumulation of microbial and periphyton resources. The observation of a more established fauna in the five-year-old ponds is therefore evidence of higher overall standing production, including the focal vector, not evidence of suppression.

Combined, the largest habitat with the longest colonization time and the most mature food base is maximized in the 30 ft square, five-year-old pond. It will have the greatest absolute standing crop and the greatest absolute emergence flux, and therefore the greatest local medical threat. The one-year-old ponds are still chemically stressful and resource-poor, and the 10 ft ponds are an order of magnitude smaller in absolute terms.
public_text.17:
E. 30 feet square, five years old

The medical threat we care about is absolute number of emerging adults from a pond, not per-area density. With depth fixed at 2 ft, habitat scales with planform area. A 30 ft square is 900 ft² vs 100 ft² for a 10 ft square, 9× surface and 9× water volume. At any comparable per-unit productivity the 30 ft pond will produce an order of magnitude more adults.

Age is working in the same direction here. These are bare cement basins with vertical sides and no sediment or macrophyte refuge. Fresh concrete leaches Ca(OH)₂ and is strongly alkaline and biologically sterile. Over years the surface weathers, pH falls toward neutral, a periphyton/biofilm develops on the walls and bottom and fine organic matter accumulates. The field observation you report — older ponds have more established insect communities — is direct empirical evidence that colonization and standing production have increased with time, not just diversity for diversity’s sake.

In this system the resource/colonization time effect dominates any putative predator suppression. The vertical cement walls limit the refugia that odonate nymphs, dytiscids and notonectids need to build up a persistent top-down guild, while the biofilm that mosquitoes feed on is monotonically increasing with pond age. A five-year-old basin therefore has both a larger, chemically stabilized habitat and multiple generations of population buildup.

That gives the 30 ft square five-year-old pond the largest absolute carrying capacity and the most reliable emergent flux of the vector. The 1-yr 30 ft pond is larger than the 10 ft ponds but it is still an early, leaching, low-resource basin with little time for population buildup, and the 10 ft ponds are too small to match the total production of the 30 ft basins.
public_text.6:
E. 30 feet square, five years old

Total medical risk is total emergent flux from a pond, i.e. per-area emergence density × habitat amount. With depth fixed at 2 ft habitat amount scales with planform area. A 30 ft square is 900 ft² vs 100 ft² for a 10 ft square, ~9× the water surface and volume, so at equal per-area productivity the 30 ft pond produces an order of magnitude more adults.

Age acts in the same direction in these cement basins. Fresh concrete is biologically sterile and strongly alkaline from Ca(OH)₂ leaching. pH falls and a periphyton/biofilm/detrital layer can develop on the vertical cement walls and bottom only with time. The field observation that the older ponds have more established insect communities is the signature of that in-situ maturation and resource accrual. That maturation gives a longer colonization window, a more stable physicochemistry and more larval food, so per-unit-area carrying capacity and realized emergence of the resident fauna, including the vector, increase with age in a permanent artificial basin.

Combining the two positive effects, largest area × most biologically and chemically mature habitat maximizes absolute standing stock and emergent output. The 30 ft square five year old pond therefore hosts the greatest absolute abundance of the study vector and the greatest local medical threat. The 30 ft one year old pond is the highest-risk young basin in a predator-release model, but in a vertical cement system pH neutralisation and biofilm accumulation with age outweigh early successional predator release, so E > C > D > A for total adult production.
public_text.20:
E. 30 feet square, five years old

Total emergent production is carrying capacity × area. Depth is fixed at 2 ft so water volume and usable wetted cement scale with planform area. A 30 ft × 30 ft pond is 900 ft² surface and 1 800 ft³ volume vs 100 ft² and 200 ft³ for a 10 ft × 10 ft pond, ~9× the habitat for oviposition and larval development at any given per-area rate. All else equal the 30 ft pond will therefore produce an order of magnitude more adults in absolute terms than a 10 ft pond.

Age acts in the same direction for total absolute abundance in these artificial cement basins. Fresh cement leaches Ca(OH)₂ and is biologically sterile; with time the surface weathers, pH falls toward neutral, a periphyton/biofilm and a detrital pool accumulate on the vertical walls and bottom, and repeated colonization builds a resident fauna. The field observation that the older ponds have more established insect communities is the signature of that in-situ maturation and resource accrual. In a permanent 2 ft deep cement basin that maturation increases larval food resources and allows multiple generations to build up a stable, resident population of the vector. The five year old ponds are therefore the most biologically developed and the most productive habitats for a resident aquatic insect.

Combined, the largest habitat quantity and the greatest degree of colonization / resource maturation maximise the absolute number of emerging adults and hence the local biting pressure / medical threat. The 30 ft square five year old pond therefore has the greatest expected total abundance of the study species. The younger large pond, 30 ft square one year old, may have a higher per-area density if the species is a classic early-successional predator-release coloniser, but it will have a lower standing crop of food and a shorter colonization window, and the 10 ft ponds are an order of magnitude smaller in total production.
public_text.12:
E. 30 feet square, five years old

Total emergence is density per unit area × area. At constant 2 ft depth usable breeding habitat scales with planform area, 30 ft × 30 ft = 900 ft² vs 10 ft × 10 ft = 100 ft², i.e. ~9× the water surface, volume and wetted cement for oviposition and larval rearing. All else equal a 30 ft pond will therefore produce an order of magnitude more adults than a 10 ft pond.

Age is positive for absolute production in these sterile cement basins. Fresh concrete leaches Ca(OH)2, is strongly alkaline and biologically sterile. Periphyton / biofilm development, pH neutralisation and detrital accrual on the vertical walls and bottom require years. The field observation that older ponds have more established insect communities is the direct evidence of that in-situ maturation and of successful multi-generation colonisation. More standing organic matter and a stable microbial food base increase larval carrying capacity and give the vector repeated opportunities to build up a resident population over five years.

Combined, the largest area with the longest time for chemical stabilisation, resource accumulation and population build-up gives the largest absolute standing stock and emergent flux. That is the 30 ft square five year old pond. The size advantage makes any 30 ft pond dominate any 10 ft pond at equal age, and the maturation / establishment advantage makes the five year old 30 ft pond dominate the one year old 30 ft pond for total adult output and therefore for local medical threat. The pioneer predator-release argument for a strictly early-successional r-strategist would favour the young large basin C for mosquito-specific per-area density, but the observation given is of greater overall insect community establishment with age, which is read here as greater absolute vector abundance in the oldest, largest permanent habitat.
public_text.21:
E. 30 feet square, five years old

Medical threat is total adult emergence, not per-area density, and both area and time are acting in the same direction for absolute production in these cement basins.

At constant 2 ft depth habitat scales with planform. A 30 ft square is 900 ft² water surface versus 100 ft² for a 10 ft square, 9× the water volume and ~6× the total wetted cement surface when you include the vertical walls, 1 140 ft² vs 180 ft² of biofilm substrate. All else equal that is an order of magnitude more oviposition and larval rearing space.

Age is positive for absolute carrying capacity here. Fresh concrete leaches Ca[OH]2, is strongly alkaline and essentially sterile. Periphyton/biofilm and fine detritus need years to accumulate on the bare cement, and pH needs time to fall to a range that supports sustained larval development. The field observation we have is that older ponds have more established insect communities. That is direct empirical evidence of higher standing production, not just more predators. The study vector is part of that established community.

In a vertical-walled cement basin there is essentially no sediment, macrophyte refuge or structural complexity for predator colonization. The predator-suppression story used to favor the young ponds assumes an odonate/dytiscid/notonectid assemblage can build up effectively on bare cement, which is questionable, and in any case the observed increase in overall insect establishment with age indicates net productivity is rising, not falling, for the community as a whole. A one-year-old basin is still resource-limited and chemically harsh; a five-year-old basin is pH-stabilized, biofilm-rich and has had multiple generations for a resident mosquito population to build up.

So per pond total emergence ≈ area × time-dependent productivity. The largest area combined with the longest time for colonization, resource accumulation and population buildup is the 30 ft square five-year-old pond. That is the greatest absolute number of emerging adults and therefore the greatest local medical threat, even if a transient per-trap density spike can be seen in brand new water.
public_text.11:
C. 30 feet square, one year old

Total emergent exposure is per-area emergence density × usable habitat. With constant 2 ft depth usable habitat scales with planform area. 30 ft × 30 ft = 900 ft² vs 10 ft × 10 ft = 100 ft², ~9× water surface and volume, and 120 ft vs 40 ft perimeter at a given age, so for any common density the 30 ft basin will produce an order of magnitude more adults in absolute terms than a 10 ft basin.

Age acts on density in the opposite direction for a classic artificial-pond disease vector. Fresh cement is sterile, high pH and low in periphyton/detritus. In the first year the basin is essentially predator/competitor poor and a r-selected coloniser mosquito can achieve a high per-area emergence. The field note that the five year old ponds have more established insect communities is the signature of pond succession in permanent cement basins: build up of periphyton/biofilm, and with it colonization by mosquito larval predators and competitors such as odonate nymphs, dytiscid and hydrophilid beetles, notonectids, and a complex grazer assemblage that provides strong biotic resistance on the essentially featureless vertical walls and bottom.

Hence per-unit-area mosquito emergence is highest in the youngest, least biologically resistant age class, 1 yr > 5 yr, and absolute production = density × area is maximised where the highest density meets the largest area. That is the largest basin still in the early successional, predator-poor stage: a 30 ft square one year old pond.

If density were assumed to increase monotonically with successional age the formal maximum under a simple area × time model would be the 30 ft square five year old pond, E, but under the pioneer mosquito boom / predator establishment dynamic that is the established expectation for disease-vector mosquitoes in permanent artificial cement basins, the youngest large basin dominates total adult production and therefore local medical threat. On a density-standardised basis any 1-yr pond > any 5-yr pond, with size irrelevant to per-area rate.
public_text.8:
E. 30 feet square, five years old

Total medical risk from a pond is total emergent production, not per-unit-area density. With depth fixed at 2 ft habitat quantity scales with planform area. 
30 ft × 30 ft = 900 ft² vs 10 ft × 10 ft = 100 ft², i.e. ≈9× water surface and ≈9× water volume for a given per-area productivity. At equal density the 30 ft basin therefore holds an order of magnitude more adult vectors than the 10 ft basin.

Age acts in the same direction in a bare cement basin. Fresh Portland cement leaches Ca(OH)₂ and is strongly alkaline and biologically sterile. pH falls and a periphyton/biofilm and fine detrital layer build up on the vertical walls and bottom over years. That is the mechanistic basis for the field observation that the older ponds have more established insect communities. On the 1–5 yr time scale in a permanent vertical-sided cement basin the limiting factors for mosquito larvae are pH neutralisation and food base development, not predator release. Food accrual and successful multi-generation colonisation increase per-unit-area carrying capacity with age in these low-nutrient artificial systems, and the observed increase in established insect communities is the signature of that in situ enrichment.

Thus both quantity and quality increase with age and size. The 30 ft square five year old pond combines the maximal area/volume with the maximal degree of chemical stabilisation, biofilm development and community establishment. It therefore has the largest absolute standing stock and emergent flux of the study species and the greatest local absolute biting pressure.

If the age effect were taken as pure predator/competitor suppression of an r-selected pioneer, per-area mosquito density would be 1 yr > 5 yr and the size advantage would still make the 30 ft 1 yr basin the largest absolute producer in absolute terms, option C. On the food/pH/colonisation basis that dominates in newly cemented permanent basins, density increases with age and E dominates C, with the 10 ft basins always subordinate.
public_text.19:
E. 30 feet square, five years old

Total medical risk is total emergent production per pond, i.e. habitat amount × per-unit-habitat production.

Habitat amount is set by planform area at constant 2 ft depth and vertical cement walls. 30 ft × 30 ft = 900 ft² water surface and 1 800 ft³ volume vs 10 ft × 10 ft = 100 ft² and 200 ft³; ~9× surface/volume and 3× perimeter, 120 ft vs 40 ft. All else equal the 30 ft pond can hold ~9× the absolute standing crop of the 10 ft pond.

Age acts in the same direction for a cement basin. Fresh concrete leaches Ca(OH)₂ and is strongly alkaline and biologically sterile. Over years pH falls toward neutral, a periphyton/biofilm and fine detrital layer develops on the cement walls and bottom, and the system can actually support aquatic life. That is exactly what you are observing: older ponds have more established insect communities. In a permanent vertical-sided cement basin with no natural sediment or macrophyte refuge, maturation is reflected in pH recovery and in-situ enrichment and colonization time, not in a classic predator-release pulse. The five-year ponds have had multiple generations for repeated colonization, oviposition and population build-up and have accumulated the microbial/detrital food base that supports filter-feeding / detritivorous mosquito larvae.

Hence per pond carrying capacity increases with both area and age. The 30 ft square five year old pond combines the maximal habitat quantity with the maximal degree of chemical stabilization and biological establishment. It will therefore support the greatest absolute number of emerging adults and the greatest local biting pressure / medical threat, even if a density-standardized trap would show the highest per-area catch in a one-year-old basin. The 10 ft ponds can never match the absolute production of a 30 ft pond at the same age, and the one-year-old ponds are still the most chemically and biologically depauperate cement habitats.
public_text.18:
C. 30 feet square, one year old.

Total emergent output = per-area emergence density × available habitat area. At constant 2 ft depth habitat scales with planform area and the wetted cement surface. A 30 ft square is 900 ft2 water surface vs 100 ft2 for a 10 ft square, ~9× the rearing volume and ~6× the total wetted cement for biofilm accrual, so at any given per-area density the 30 ft basin will produce an order of magnitude more adults in absolute terms than a 10 ft basin.

Age acts on per-area density. These are newly built, vertical-sided cement basins with no sediment or macrophyte refuge. Fresh concrete is sterile and initially predator/competitor poor. Early succession is therefore dominated by r-selected pioneer colonisers. The field note that the older ponds have more established insect communities is the signature of successional biotic resistance: odonate nymphs, dytiscids, notonectids, copepods and an increasingly complex grazer/competitor assemblage build up over years. In a basin with vertical walls the effect of that maturation is top-down / exploitative suppression of mosquito larvae rather than a sustained increase in mosquito-specific carrying capacity, because there is essentially no organic sediment pool to draw on.

Hence per-area emergence density of a pioneer disease-vector mosquito is expected to be highest in the youngest, least biologically controlled ponds and to decline with pond age as predators/competitors accumulate, even though total insect community biomass/diversity rises. Per-area: 1 yr > 5 yr. Absolute: 30 ft >> 10 ft.

The combination that maximises absolute production is therefore the largest habitat with the youngest, predator-poor successional stage, i.e. the 30 ft square one-year-old pond. A 30 ft five-year-old pond has the area advantage but the per-area mosquito density is suppressed by the established community; a 10 ft pond can never match the absolute output of a 30 ft pond at the same age. If sampling is standardised to the fixed footprint of a single emergence trap the density effect dominates and any 1-yr pond out-samples any 5-yr pond, with 30 ft vs 10 ft being irrelevant to per-area rate. The greatest medical exposure risk in absolute terms remains the large young basin.
public_text.10:
C. 30 feet square, one year old

For a fixed depth the absolute production that a pond can put out is
per-unit-area emergence density × planform area, and the per-unit-area
density of a pioneer disease-vector mosquito in these artificial cement
basins is a decreasing function of successional age.

The basins are 2 ft deep with vertical cement sides and bottoms. Usable
oviposition / emergence habitat therefore scales essentially with plan
area: 10 ft × 10 ft = 100 ft² vs 30 ft × 30 ft = 900 ft², ≈9× habitat
volume / surface for the large basin at the same depth. At equal density
the 30 ft basin will therefore always support ≈9× the absolute number of
emerging adults of a 10 ft basin.

Age acts on density in the opposite direction. New concrete is
essentially sterile and predator-poor; the first year is a classic
pioneer phase for r-selected container / artificial-pond mosquitoes. You
note that the older ponds have more established insect communities. In a
permanent vertical-sided cement basin that establishment is the build-up
of periphyton / biofilm and, more importantly for a mosquito, of a
resident predator / competitor guild – odonate nymphs, dytiscid and
hydrophilid beetles, notonectids / naucorids, copepods and competing
chironomid/filter feeders – with essentially no macrophyte or sediment
refuge for larvae. The net effect is biotic resistance: per-area
emergence density of an early-colonising vector is highest when the basin
is young and predator / competitor pressure is minimal and declines as
the community matures, even though total insect biomass / diversity rises
with age.

Hence per area: 1 yr > 5 yr. Absolute abundance = density × area, so
the largest area that retains the young, low-resistance density is
maximal. That is the 30 ft square, 1-yr-old basin.

On a standardized emergence-trap basis the trap samples a fixed water
area, so size drops out and any 1-yr pond out-catches any 5-yr pond for
a pioneer mosquito. In terms of absolute pond-level production and
therefore local medical exposure the 9× area advantage of the 30 ft basin
is retained on top of the young-age density advantage, giving the 30 ft
square one year old pond the greatest expected total emergence. If the
vector were a late-successional component of the mature community the
sign of the age effect would reverse and E would be the formal maximum;
under the classic early-successional mosquito pulse / predator-
establishment dynamic the young large basin dominates.

3.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The ponds are 2 ft deep with vertical cement sides/bottoms, so habitat scales with planform area at constant depth. 30 ft square = 900 ft² water surface, 10 ft square = 100 ft², ~9× surface/volume. Wetted cement including walls is side² + 4·side·depth ≈ 1 140 ft² vs 180 ft², ~6.3×.

Total adult production = per-area emergence density × area. Age effect is the contested sign.

Pro-C, 30 ft square one year old, argument:
* Cement basins start sterile/alkaline from Ca(OH)2 leach, low periphyton/biofilm initially.
* Early successional, predator-poor phase favors r-selected colonising/disease-vector mosquitoes; per-area density highest in young ponds.
* Succession builds predators/competitors – odonate nymphs, dytiscids, notonectids, hemipterans, copepods – that suppress mosquito larvae in 5-yr ponds. “More established insect communities” = biotic resistance.
* Hence density young > old. Area advantage of 30 ft dominates 10 ft. Largest young basin gives greatest absolute emergence: 30 ft × 1 yr > 30 ft × 5 yr > 10 ft × 1 yr > 10 ft × 5 yr.
* If sampling were standardized to trap area, density alone would favor any 1-yr pond over 5-yr.

Pro-E, 30 ft square five years old, argument:
* Total standing crop scales with area × carrying capacity, and carrying capacity in these artificial cement basins increases with time as periphyton/biofilm develops, pH falls to near neutral, detritus accumulates, and microbial food base stabilizes.
* “More established insect communities” in older ponds is taken as evidence of successful colonization, resource maturation and higher overall insect productivity, including the focal vector.
* Five years allows multiple generations, persistent larval food, colonization window, stable thermal regime. Larger area gives ~9× habitat.
* Combined maximal area + maximal maturation gives maximal absolute standing stock/emergent flux, even if per-unit-area density is sometimes higher early.
* Some note wetted cement area = side² + 4·side·depth, also larger for 30 ft.

Disagreement is sign of age effect on mosquito-specific abundance: pioneer pulse with predator release and density decline with succession vs. resource accumulation and colonization time increasing suitability with age.

Current round distribution: strong minority C 1,10,11,15,18,4 et al.; majority E 12,13,14,16,17,19,2,20,21,3,5,6,7,8,9 et al. No support for B, A or D as maximal. Most explicitly frame threat as absolute number of adults per pond, not per-area density.

Unresolved remains life history of the study vector and how to interpret “more established insect communities”. If vector is classic early coloniser of sterile artificial water, C is correct; if it benefits from mature biofilm/resource buildup and established community, E is correct. The question emphasizes observed more established insect communities in older ponds and asks for greatest absolute abundance/medical threat, not per-area density. Need to decide which interpretation of “established” to apply to the vector specifically.

Earlier points remain: depth constant, size dominates absolute numbers; predator/competitor build-up logic vs pH/ biofilm maturation logic; perimeter 120 ft vs 40 ft; 9× volume advantage for 30 ft.

Potential error/correction noted: predator establishment in featureless vertical cement may be limited, so food/pH may dominate over top-down control on 1–5 yr scale.

11.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The ponds are 2 ft deep with vertical cement sides/bottoms, so usable habitat scales with planform area: 10 ft square = 100 ft², 30 ft square = 900 ft² ≈9× surface and volume, perimeter 40 ft vs 120 ft. Depth constant, so area dominates absolute carrying capacity.

Age effect is the crux and remains disputed.

C camp: disease-vector mosquito is an early-colonising r-selected pioneer of artificial low-nutrient cement basins. Fresh concrete is sterile/alkaline; first year = minimal periphyton, minimal predator/competitor guild, high per-area mosquito density. Succession builds odonate nymphs, dytiscids, notonectids, chironomid competitors etc. in 5-yr ponds → biotic resistance increases with age, so per-area emergence density is 1-yr > 5-yr. Total production = density × area. Area dominates size effect, density dominates age effect downward. Max absolute adults = largest area in youngest age class: 30 ft square, one year old, option C. Even per-area, any 1-yr pond > any 5-yr pond; absolute threat dominated by 30 ft vs 10 ft. Trap standardized to area → size drops out, 1-yr > 5-yr.

E camp: maturation increases resources and persistence. Over 5 yr pH falls, periphyton/biofilm and detrital accumulation develop on cement, and repeated colonization allows build-up of stable resident fauna. Larger area gives 9× carrying capacity; older age gives more food and more generations to establish. Older ponds having “more established insect communities” is read as higher total insect productivity and higher absolute vector standing stock. Max absolute adults = largest and oldest: 30 ft square, five years old, option E. On this view age increases per-unit-area production, reinforcing area advantage. Predator build-up is limited by lack of macrophyte/sediment refuge in vertical cement; food/pH limitation dominates year 1-5.

Unresolved: life-history of focal vector. If classic container/artificial-pond pioneer suppressed by predators, C is correct. If it benefits from habitat conditioning and persistence, E is correct. Observation that older ponds have more established insect communities is used by C as evidence of predator/competitor buildup and by E as evidence of habitat maturation and vector buildup.

Current colleague split has shifted toward E in round 1. Several C proponents keep predator-release mechanism, several E proponents keep resource-accumulation/persistence mechanism. Need decide which successional effect dominates for a disease-vector mosquito in permanent cement ponds, and whether the question asks for absolute total abundance vs density-standardized trap catch.

6.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The question is total absolute adult emergence = per-area emergence density × habitat amount. Habitat amount at fixed 2 ft depth and vertical cement sides scales with planform area: 10 ft square = 100 ft², 30 ft square = 900 ft² ≈9× surface/volume, ~3× perimeter. Size therefore dominates absolute numbers at equal density.

Age effect is the contested driver of per-area density.

C camp – 30 ft square, one year old – per-area density of a pioneer disease-vector mosquito is highest early in succession. Fresh cement basins are essentially sterile, predator/competitor poor, and r-selected colonisers boom before odonate nymphs, dytiscids, notonectids etc. build up. The field note “older ponds have more established insect communities” is read as biotic resistance building with time, so per-area emergence declines with age. Total abundance = density × area, so largest area + youngest least resistant age = max absolute output. On a trap-standardised basis any 1-yr pond > any 5-yr pond; for absolute threat 30 ft 1-yr dominates.

E camp – 30 ft square, five years old – per-area productivity increases with age in these cement systems. Fresh concrete leaches Ca(OH)₂, is strongly alkaline and biologically sterile; pH falls to near neutral and periphyton/biofilm/detrital accrual on walls/bottom develops over years. The observation that older ponds have more established insect communities is taken as in-situ enrichment, chemical stabilisation and multi-generation colonisation. Larger area gives ~9× carrying capacity; older age gives higher resource availability and stable breeding. Combined largest + oldest maximises absolute standing stock and emergent flux, even if per-unit-area mosquito density were modestly suppressed by predators.

Key tensions retained from prior rounds:
* Density vs total abundance: trap-standardised density favours young ponds; absolute adult output favours large area.
* Successional predator/competitor suppression vs resource/pH maturation: does cement leaching/pH and biofilm development increase vector suitability faster than predator buildup decreases it?
* Vertical cement with no sediment/macrophyte refuge limits predator refugia and makes food/pH limitation plausible in year 1.
* Unresolved species ecology: pioneer r-selected container/artificial-pond mosquito vs late-successional/resource-tracking taxon.

Round 1 public responses show a clear split but a numerical majority for E, ~15 vs ~6 for C. The E arguments now repeatedly stress chemical maturation and pH neutralisation as the primary constraint in year 1, and read “more established insect communities” as evidence of higher total productivity rather than just predator accumulation. C arguments remain consistent on early-successional predator-release and per-area density peak at 1 yr.

My current understanding: size advantage is unambiguous, area 9×. Age sign is plausibly positive for total production in permanent cement basins because pH leaching and sterile substrate make year 1 low resource/low suitability, and predator build-up in a featureless vertical-walled box is slower than biofilm accrual. That points to E, 30 ft square five years old, as the greatest absolute medical threat, with C, 30 ft square one year old, the best alternative if the study species is a strict early-successional pioneer whose density declines sharply with predator establishment.

Unresolved: actual pH/time course for these basins, species-specific tolerance to alkalinity, and quantitative trade-off between ~9× area gain vs plausible per-area density decline from 1 to 5 yr.

8.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The area effect is now consensus: depth 2 ft constant, vertical cement sides → usable habitat scales with planform area. 30 ft × 30 ft = 900 ft² vs 10 ft × 10 ft = 100 ft², ≈9× water surface/volume, ≈3× perimeter. At equal per-area density the 30 ft basin always produces ~9× the absolute adults of a 10 ft basin.

Age effect remains contested and drives the C vs E split.

Successional suppression / pioneer mosquito view, now argued by Colleagues 1,10,11,15,18,4:
* Fresh cement is sterile, high pH from Ca(OH)₂ leach, low periphyton/biofilm. Year 1 is predator/competitor poor.
* Field note “older ponds have more established insect communities” = build-up of biotic resistance: odonate nymphs, dytiscids, hydrophilids, notonectids, copepods, chironomid competitors.
* In a featureless vertical-walled basin there is little macrophyte/sediment refuge, so top-down/exploitative control rises with age while total insect biomass/diversity rises.
* For an r-selected artificial-water / container-type vector per-area emergence density is 1 yr > 5 yr. Absolute abundance = density × area, so the highest total adult output is largest area + youngest low-resistance age: 30 ft square, one year old, option C. On a density-standardised trap size drops out and any 1-yr pond > any 5-yr pond.

Maturation / resource accumulation view, now argued by Colleagues 12,13,14,16,17,19,2,20,21,3,5,6,7,8,9:
* Fresh concrete is chemically harsh and biologically sterile; pH neutralisation, periphyton/biofilm and fine detrital accrual on walls/bottom require years.
* Older ponds having more established insect communities is read as in-situ enrichment and successful multi-generation colonisation, i.e. higher standing production.
* Food limitation and chemical instability dominate years 1–5 in permanent cement basins; predator build-up is limited by lack of refugia. Per-unit-area carrying capacity and realized emergence increase with age, so 5 yr > 1 yr.
* Combined with the 9× area advantage, total absolute emergence and therefore local medical threat is maximised by the largest oldest basin: 30 ft square, five years old, option E. Even if per-area density were slightly higher in year 1, the area + maturation gain outweighs it for total adults.

Observed shifts in round 1: Colleague 10 and 11 moved from E to C; Colleague 3 moved from C to E. The core disagreement is the sign of age on the focal vector specifically: does “more established insect communities” mean more predators/competitors suppressing a pioneer vector, or more resource accrual / pH stabilisation increasing vector productivity? Cement vertical sides limit classic littoral predator refugia, which supports the maturation argument, but the same featurelessness also makes larvae exposed to any predators that do establish, supporting the suppression argument.

reflection_text.6:
The question is total absolute adult emergence = per-area emergence density × habitat amount. Habitat amount at fixed 2 ft depth and vertical cement sides scales with planform area: 10 ft square = 100 ft², 30 ft square = 900 ft² ≈9× surface/volume, ~3× perimeter. Size therefore dominates absolute numbers at equal density.

Age effect is the contested driver of per-area density.

C camp – 30 ft square, one year old – per-area density of a pioneer disease-vector mosquito is highest early in succession. Fresh cement basins are essentially sterile, predator/competitor poor, and r-selected colonisers boom before odonate nymphs, dytiscids, notonectids etc. build up. The field note “older ponds have more established insect communities” is read as biotic resistance building with time, so per-area emergence declines with age. Total abundance = density × area, so largest area + youngest least resistant age = max absolute output. On a trap-standardised basis any 1-yr pond > any 5-yr pond; for absolute threat 30 ft 1-yr dominates.

E camp – 30 ft square, five years old – per-area productivity increases with age in these cement systems. Larger area gives ~9× carrying capacity; older age gives higher resource availability and stable breeding. Combined largest + oldest maximises absolute standing stock and emergent flux, even if per-unit-area mosquito density were modestly suppressed by predators.

The field note “older ponds have more established insect communities” is read as biotic resistance increasing with succession. Per-area density 1 yr > 5 yr. Absolute abundance = density × area, so the largest young basin maximizes total adults: 30 ft square one year old, C. Per-trap density is then any 1-yr pond > any 5-yr pond.

* Resource-maturation / establishment. Fresh concrete is alkaline and biologically sterile; pH neutralisation, periphyton/biofilm and fine detrital accrual on walls/bottom take years. The same field note is read as in-situ enrichment and successful multi-generation colonisation: more standing organic matter, stable chemistry and a resident fauna. In a permanent vertical cement basin with no macrophyte/sediment refuge, food/chemical limitation dominates the 1–5 yr window and predator build-up is limited by habitat complexity. Per-unit-area and total productivity increase with age. Combined with area, largest oldest pond maximises absolute standing stock: 30 ft square five years old, E.

Unresolved that remains decisive: species identity of the vector – container/ephemeral-water Aedes-type pioneer vs a permanent-water Culex-type that tracks biofilm/detritus; and how “greatest medical threat” is operationalised with one emergence trap. If threat = catch per standardized trap footprint, size drops out and age sign decides per-area density.

Mechanistically concrete leaching and resource accrual provide a strong a priori reason for age to increase productivity in these bare cement basins, and the field observation of more established communities is most parsimoniously an increase in standing production, not just predator suppression. That pushes weight toward E, 30 ft square five years old, while the classic predator-release pioneer model remains a viable alternative that would make C correct. E. 30 feet square, five years old

Medical threat is total adult emergence per pond, i.e. per-area realized productivity × habitat amount.

Habitat amount at fixed 2 ft depth and vertical cement sides scales with planform area. 30 ft × 30 ft = 900 ft² water surface and ~1,800 ft³ volume vs 10 ft × 10 ft = 100 ft² and ~200 ft³, ~9× surface/volume and ~3× perimeter. At any comparable per-unit productivity a 30 ft basin will always deliver an order of magnitude more adults than a 10 ft basin, so any 30 ft pond dominates any 10 ft pond in absolute terms.

Age acts in the same positive direction for absolute production in these bare cement basins. Five years gives multiple generations of colonization and resident population build-up.

The field observation that older ponds have more established insect communities is direct empirical evidence of that chemical maturation and resource accrual. It is an increase in standing aquatic production, not just diversity for diversity’s sake. Hence both quantity and quality increase with size and age. The largest habitat combined with the longest time for pH stabilization, biofilm development and multi-generation establishment maximizes absolute standing stock and emergent flux. That is the 30 ft square five year old pond.

PRIVATE REFLECTION: The ponds are 2 ft deep with vertical cement sides/bottoms so usable habitat scales with planform area: 10 ft square =100 ft², 30 ft square =900 ft², ~9× surface/volume; perimeter also ~3×. Depth constant means total carrying capacity is area × per-area productivity.

Two mechanistic readings remain in tension:

Five years allows multiple generations, chemical stabilisation and persistent food base. Larger area gives ~9× oviposition habitat.
